title: “TEST ME IN THIS” — THE VERSE PROSPERITY PREACHERS LOVE TO QUOTE… BUT WHAT DID GOD ACTUALLY PROMISE?
paragraphs:
“TEST ME IN THIS” — THE VERSE PROSPERITY PREACHERS LOVE TO QUOTE… BUT WHAT DID GOD ACTUALLY PROMISE?
Malachi 3:10 contains one of Scripture’s most astonishing invitations from God. But if you have been told it means, “Give God money and He is obligated to make you rich,” you need to read what comes before it, what comes after it—and what the Hebrew actually says.
There is a sentence in the Bible that almost sounds dangerous when you first hear it.
And because those words appear beside a promise about blessing, Malachi 3:10 has become one of the most quoted verses whenever Christians talk about money.
You may have heard it before.
Then wait for God to multiply it.

Sometimes the message becomes even more specific: give God ten percent and He will give you more money back. Give sacrificially and your breakthrough will arrive. Put money into the offering and heaven will become obligated to increase your bank account.
And somewhere in the middle of all that excitement sits Malachi 3:10.
But there is a question every follower of Jesus must be willing to ask:
Is that actually what God said?
Because Scripture is too holy to become a sales technique.
God's promises are too precious to become advertising slogans.

And people who are desperate, frightened, unemployed, buried in debt, caring for sick relatives, wondering how they will feed their children, or praying through financial disaster are too precious to be handed promises God never made.
So come closer to the text.
Not to find an excuse for selfishness.
Not to argue about percentages while protecting our wallets.
Come because sometimes the difference between biblical faith and spiritual manipulation is simply this:
“Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in My house. Test Me in this…”
The Hebrew behind that famous phrase is striking:
The key word is בְּחָנוּנִי — bechanuni, from the Hebrew root בחן — bachan.
It carries the idea of examining, testing, trying, or proving.
The force of the statement really is extraordinary.
God genuinely tells His covenant people to test Him in this matter.
We should not explain the words away merely because others have abused them.
But notice what God does not say.
“Send money to a preacher and I guarantee you will become wealthy.”
“Give ten percent and I will return one hundred percent.”
“Anyone who tithes will receive a larger house, a better car, a promotion, or financial independence.”
Those promises are not in the verse.
אִם־לֹא אֶפְתַּח לָכֶם אֵת אֲרֻבּוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם
Im-lo eftach lakhem et arubbot hashamayim…
God speaks of opening for them the “windows” or floodgates of heaven and pouring out blessing.
But now we must ask the question that changes everything:
Who is God speaking to, and what crisis is happening?
The surrounding passage is not a motivational speech about becoming financially successful.

Malachi speaks about defective sacrifices, corrupt priests, marital unfaithfulness, injustice, exploitation, withholding from God, and a people whose relationship with Him had become spiritually diseased.
Immediately before the famous “test Me” invitation comes another invitation that prosperity preaching can easily rush past:
“Return to Me, and I will return to you.”
There is the heartbeat of Malachi.
The issue underneath their money was their relationship with God.
Their hearts were the deeper problem.
This is not God dangling wealth before strangers.
This is the covenant Lord confronting His covenant people and calling them back to faithfulness.
The tithe was brought into the storehouse so there would be food in God's house.
The following verse speaks explicitly about the produce of the land and the vine in the field.

The “windows of heaven” language was not floating in an abstract financial universe. Israel lived from the land. Rain mattered. Harvest mattered. Crops mattered. Covenant blessing and covenant judgment had already been described to Israel in agricultural terms.
The people hearing Malachi would not naturally have imagined stock portfolios, luxury automobiles, six-figure salaries, investment properties, or oversized checks arriving unexpectedly in the mail.
They would have thought about something much more immediate.
God was telling His people that He remained faithful even while exposing their unfaithfulness.
And perhaps that is where this passage becomes much more beautiful than the get-rich version.
Because the real miracle in Malachi 3 is not merely that God can open heaven.
It is that rebellious people are being invited to return.
People who had failed Him were being called back to Him.
People who had withheld from Him were still hearing His voice.
People who deserved judgment were being offered restoration.
That sounds strangely familiar, doesn't it?
Because eventually the story of Scripture takes us somewhere beyond a storehouse.
It takes us to a hill outside Jerusalem.
And there we discover the deepest treasure Christianity has ever proclaimed:
God's greatest gift to sinners was not money.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross so that Christianity could become a strategy for acquiring possessions.
He went to the cross because we were sinners who needed reconciliation with God.
“Give God enough and eventually He will make you rich.”
You could never purchase God's mercy, so Christ purchased your redemption with His blood.
That changes everything about Christian giving.
We no longer give because we think God is a cosmic investment account.
We give because we have already received something money could never buy.
And suddenly generosity stops being a transaction.
That does not mean the New Testament teaches timid generosity.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 9 that whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly and whoever sows generously will reap generously.
That sounds almost like the prosperity message—until you keep reading.
Paul says each believer should give what he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And then Paul explains the purpose of God's provision.
But so that, having sufficiency, believers may abound in every good work.
There is a universe of difference between those two messages.
“God supplies so you can keep becoming useful in His hands.”
One puts wealth at the center.
The other puts grace at the center.
One asks, “How much will God give me back?”
The other asks, “Lord, what can You do through everything You have entrusted to me?”
Christian generosity is not less radical than transactional giving.
Because once Jesus owns your heart, the question is no longer merely whether God gets ten percent.
And this is where Malachi 3:10 can expose both sides of our hearts.
It exposes the preacher who turns blessing into bait.
But it can also expose the Christian who uses criticism of prosperity theology as permission to become stingy.
We cannot say, “Malachi isn't a get-rich formula,” and then close our wallets with relief.
Jesus does not rescue us from manipulative giving so we can become comfortable consumers.
He rescues us so we can become joyful disciples.
Caring for widows and vulnerable people matters.
Using money for eternal purposes matters.
But our giving must never become an attempt to control God.
You cannot manipulate the Almighty with an offering.
You cannot place heaven in your debt.
You cannot hand God a seed offering and force Him to sign a contract promising financial wealth.
God is not a slot machine with Bible verses written across the front.
And if you have ever given money believing that God was required to make you wealthy afterward—and the wealth never came—hear this carefully.
The failure of that formula does not mean God failed you.
It may mean someone promised you something God never promised.
Perhaps you emptied money you desperately needed because someone told you that your miracle depended upon it.
Perhaps you waited for the “hundredfold return.”
Perhaps you wondered whether your faith was too small.
Perhaps you secretly wondered whether God had forgotten you.
And perhaps you have been carrying shame ever since.
Christian faith has never promised that obedience will eliminate suffering.
The apostles followed Christ and suffered.
Faithful believers throughout history have died without becoming wealthy.
Our Savior Himself warned against storing up treasures on earth and taught His disciples to seek first the kingdom of God.
Jesus is not ashamed of the believer who dies without becoming rich.
This does not mean God cannot prosper someone materially.
Every legitimate possession is ultimately under His providence.
He can provide through another believer.
He can provide far beyond what you expected.
We should never make our theology so reactionary that we become embarrassed by God's generosity.
But provision is not the same thing as a guaranteed path to wealth.
And blessing is bigger than money.
Sometimes it looks like contentment when provision is small.
Sometimes it looks like the strength to survive what you prayed would disappear.
Sometimes it looks like brothers and sisters carrying you when you cannot carry yourself.
Sometimes it looks like bread arriving exactly when you need bread.
Sometimes it looks like God removing the idol you were begging Him to increase.
Sometimes the blessing is not that God puts more into your hand.
Sometimes the blessing is that He breaks money's grip on your heart.
Imagine someone who once measured his worth by what he owned.
People became more important than status.
The person whose bank account doubled while his heart moved farther from God?
Or the person whose possessions became servants instead of masters?
Jesus once asked what it profits someone to gain the whole world and lose his soul.
That question destroys every version of Christianity that makes material accumulation the final evidence of divine favor.
Because you can gain the world and still be bankrupt before God.
And you can have very little while possessing treasure thieves cannot steal.
So what does “Test Me in this” mean for us?
It means we must first let Malachi speak where Malachi actually speaks.
Into a call to repentance and restored faithfulness.
We should not rip one sentence out of that world and transform it into a universal Christian guarantee that every monetary gift produces greater monetary wealth.
But neither should we domesticate the God revealed there.
Still Lord over everything we possess.
Still calling His people away from selfishness.
And the entire biblical story still teaches us that trusting God frees us to live with open hands.
That distinction could save someone from years of spiritual confusion.
You do not give to make God love you.
You give because in Christ you have encountered a love you could never purchase.
You do not give to purchase salvation.
You do not give to force God to bless you.
You give because everything you possess already exists under His mercy.
You do not give because someone frightened you into believing your miracle has a price tag.
Sacrificially when God calls for sacrifice.
And with Christ—not money—at the center.
Maybe that is the test we desperately need today.
“Can I give enough to make God increase my income?”
“Do I trust Jesus enough that money no longer gets to be my god?”
Now the passage has reached us.
Because you can condemn prosperity preachers all day and still worship money.
You can know the Hebrew and still be greedy.
You can understand covenant theology and still ignore the poor.
You can correctly explain Malachi 3 and still refuse to surrender your wallet to Christ.
Correct interpretation should not produce colder hearts.
When God blesses you, do you immediately ask what you can buy—or do you sometimes ask whom you can bless?
When you see someone suffering, does compassion ever become action?
When Gospel ministry genuinely feeds souls, do you merely consume it, or do you help carry it?
When biblical truth strengthens you, do you keep scrolling—or do you help that truth reach somebody who is barely holding onto faith?
Because there are forms of generosity that do not begin with a credit card.
You can support faithful Gospel ministry.
You can send a biblical article to the person who desperately needs it.
You can make it a doorway through which somebody encounters Jesus.
You may need to return to these words the next time someone uses Malachi 3:10 to pressure you with a promise God never made.
Don't use truth as a weapon. Use it as a lamp.
And if this convicted your own heart—not somebody else's—be honest.
Not because a comment earns blessing.
Not because typing words proves your faith.
But sometimes publicly putting language around what God is exposing in us becomes a small moment of honesty.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, then help us keep putting Christ-centered biblical truth in front of people who desperately need it.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
Not because an algorithm glorifies God.
And certainly not because you can purchase His blessing by promoting a ministry.
Someone may be secretly furious with God because a financial “seed” never produced the promised miracle.
Someone may be walking away from Christianity because they were introduced to a transaction instead of a Savior.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing the favor of God.
Jesus already settled the question of whether grace can be bought.
You simply were not the One who paid it.
That is why the final destination of Malachi 3:10 should never be your bank account.
God was confronting people who had forgotten whose they were.
And centuries later, Christ came for people who had done far worse than withhold a tithe.
And He did not tell us to purchase our way home.
And now the invitation is infinitely greater than:
“Give Me something and see whether I will make you wealthy.”
Because perhaps the greatest “open heaven” you will ever experience is not money pouring into your hands.
Perhaps it is finally realizing that through Jesus Christ, sinners who deserved judgment have been welcomed home.
That is wealth Wall Street cannot measure.
That is treasure death cannot confiscate.
That is blessing no recession can erase.
So the next time someone quotes:
Remember that God's faithfulness is real.
Remember that Scripture must never become a fundraising weapon.
Because Christianity was never the scandalous story of poor people learning how to manipulate God into making them rich.
It is the scandalous story of the infinitely rich Son of God giving Himself for spiritually bankrupt sinners so that rebels could become children of the King.
And maybe tonight the question is no longer whether God will open heaven if you give Him enough.
Maybe the question is whether you will finally open your hands because He has already given you Christ.
Save it before another out-of-context promise makes you forget the whole story.
You were never meant to use God to get treasure. In Christ, you discover that God Himself is the Treasure.
